title: Statistical Studies, Sampling, and Margin of Error
seo_title: Sampling, Experiments and Margin of Error Worksheet (Algebra 2, S-IC) | 100 Questions with Answers
standard_text: Use data from a sample survey to estimate a population mean or proportion; develop a margin of error through the use of simulation models for random sampling.
meta_desc: Free Algebra 2 worksheet on statistical studies: surveys, observational studies and experiments, sampling bias, margin of error 1/√n, confidence intervals and simulation. 100 questions.
key_big: Only randomized experiments can show cause and effect.
key_sub: Margin of error ≈ 1/√n. Larger random samples are more precise.
body_html:
How it works

  • A sample survey asks a sample questions. An observational study watches groups that already exist. An experiment assigns treatments, ideally at random, and is the only one of the three that can show cause and effect.
  • A random sample represents the population. Convenience and voluntary response samples are usually biased.
  • For a random sample of size n, the margin of error for a proportion is about 1/√n. The interval sample result ± margin of error likely contains the true value.
  • In an experiment, a simulation of random re-assignments shows how often a difference happens by chance. A rare result (about 5% or less) is evidence of a real effect.
Example

A random sample of 900 people finds 58% like a plan. Give an interval for the true percent.

1/√900 = 1/30 ≈ 3.3%

58% ± 3.3%

Answer: 54.7% to 61.3%

Example

How does the margin of error change if the sample size goes from 400 to 1,600?

The size is 4 times as large

√4 = 2

Answer: It is cut in half

Common mistakes

  • Calling an observational study an experiment. Experiments assign the treatment.
  • Trusting a large voluntary response sample. Size does not fix bias.
  • Thinking a larger margin of error is more precise. Smaller is more precise.
  • Claiming that one variable causes another from an observational study.

faq.q: What is the difference between an observational study and an experiment?
faq.a: In an experiment the researcher assigns the treatments; in an observational study the researcher only observes groups that already exist.

faq.q: How do you estimate the margin of error?
faq.a: For a random sample of size n, the margin of error for a proportion is about 1/√n. For n = 400, that is 1/20 = 5%.
Any method that favors some members of the population, such as asking only volunteers or only people who are easy to reach.

faq.q: What does a simulation show in an experiment?
faq.a: How often a difference as large as the one observed happens by chance alone. If it is rare, the treatment likely had an effect.

items.q: What type of study is this? A company randomly gives half of its stores a new layout and compares sales with the other half.
items.e: The researcher assigns treatments (randomly) and measures the effect. Experiment.

items.q: What is a census?
c: Collecting data from every member of the population
Collecting data from a random sample
items.e: A census includes the whole population, not a sample. Collecting data from every member of the population.

items.q: Which type of study can show that one variable causes a change in another?
items.e: Only random assignment of treatments balances the other factors, so differences can be blamed on the treatment. A randomized experiment.

items.q: A study finds that people who sleep more have higher grades. Can we say sleep causes higher grades?
c: No, because grades cannot be measured
Yes, because the result was large
Yes, because the sample was random
No, it is an observational study, so it shows only an association
items.e: Other factors could explain both. Without random assignment, correlation does not show causation. No, it is an observational study, so it shows only an association.

items.q: Which question is worded in a biased way?

How many hours do you sleep on a school night?
Which sport do you play most often?
Don't you agree that the unfair tax should be removed?
items.e: The word "unfair" and "don't you agree" push people toward one answer. Don't you agree that the unfair tax should be removed?.

items.q: What does a margin of error describe?
c: The exact error in the result
The number of mistakes in the survey
How much a sample result is likely to differ from the true population value
items.e: It describes random sampling variation, not bias. How much a sample result is likely to differ from the true population value.

items.q: Why do pollsters report a margin of error?
c: Because the population changes every day
Because different random samples give slightly different results
Because they made a calculation mistake
items.e: Sample results vary from sample to sample, so an interval is more honest than one number. Because different random samples give slightly different results.

items.q: A poll says 52% ± 4% of voters support a candidate. What can we conclude?
c: The true support is likely between 48% and 56%, so the race is too close to call
Exactly 52% of all voters support the candidate
items.e: The interval includes values below 50%. The true support is likely between 48% and 56%, so the race is too close to call.

The difference in an experiment was 6 points. In 100 random re-assignments of the same data, a difference at least that large happened 2 times. What does this suggest?
c: Nothing can be concluded from a simulation
The difference is likely due to chance
The treatment definitely caused the difference in every person
The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so the treatment probably had an effect
items.e: A result that happens in only about 2% of random re-assignments is rare (usually 5% or less counts as significant). The difference is unlikely to be due to chance alone, so the treatment probably had an effect.
